name: snow-covered Roman-style stone town wall ring, 3/4 top-down (16px tiles): wall-walk tops two tiles deep seen from above (flagstone walkway with crenellated parapets), four-tile-high weathered ashlar front faces below the north and south walls, two-tile-wide west and east walls seen from above, a gatehouse with an open round arch tunnel, a gatehouse with closed wooden doors, square towers rising above the wall with crenellated top platforms (trapdoor and pennant, brazier, stone balls and crates; each tower's face has a different arrangement of arrow slits and a barred window), stone stairs up the inner face, a road passing under the west wall through a postern gate tower, ground shadows

answer.evidence: Column x=208 shows a crenellated parapet and snow flagstone wall-walk at rows 49-81 (about 33 rows), then a lighter edge line at row 82 and dark eave shadow at row 83. Below it is an ashlar front face of about 60 rows (rows 84-143). The towers repeat this pattern: platforms (x=112 rows 17-43) end in a dark edge/eave band at rows 44-48, then a stone face. The gatehouses have top platforms above their arched and door faces. The west and east wall segments are seen from above as two-tile walkways. The structure has clear tops and tall front faces, so it reads as three-quarter.

styleAnswer.evidence: The ashlar faces are shaded stone by stone, in about 5 steps from snow-white cap through light and mid grey to dark mortar and a deep base course. The stone ramp is comparable to the references' roof and wall ramps. Outlines and joints are cool-tinted dark grey, not neutral black: only 3% of dark edge pixels are neutral, against 7% and 9% for the references. Forms are separated mostly by value, which matches the Beodeul approach. Measured density is 11 visible tones per tile, between the references' 12 and 10. Near-flat coverage is 19%, against 0% for both references. That comes mainly from the pale-blue snow walkways, tower platforms and the road, which carry only sparse speckle. This is the weak point, but the stone faces, stairs, doors, banners and braziers carry enough grain and variation that it reads as a modest gap, not a sticker look. Overall it is slightly less rich than the references but would sit acceptably beside them.

answer.evidence: The main body is the town wall ring. The north wall has a wide snow-covered walkway band (about rows 50-81) with crenellated parapets at the top. It ends in a front-edge line at row 82 (L=176) with dark eave shadow at row 83 (L=90). Below that is a tall ashlar front face (about rows 84-143, 60 or more rows) with the stone courses. The towers and both gatehouses each show their own crenellated top platform, with an edge line and shadow, above their front faces. The west and east walls are seen from above as walkways. The south wall repeats the same walkway, edge line and face structure. The pennant, brazier, crates and balls on the platforms are decor. No isometric receding side face is drawn, only the south faces.

styleAnswer.evidence: The ashlar faces are shaded block by block in about 5 grey steps, with mortar lines, a darker plinth and a lighter coping, so the stone is not a flat fill. The snow carries sparse speckle and the blue-grey shadow bands on the wall-walks add value variation. Visible tones per 16x16 tile are 11, against 12 and 10 for the references, so tile density is at par. Only 3% of dark edge pixels are neutral, so the outlines lean toward the grey-brown of the adjacent stone and are not a black sticker line. Near-flat coverage is 19% against 0% for the references. That comes mostly from the pale snow patches, the road and the dark tunnel interior, and it is the weakest point. Total colours are low (49 against 66 and 185), so the texture is less varied than Beodeul's. Even so, at this scale the piece would sit acceptably beside the references.

answer.evidence: Column x=208 shows the north wall-walk as a deep top band: outline at row 48, white parapet and crenel rows 49-59, and a snow flagstone walkway at rows 60-81 (about 34 rows in all). A 1-row lighter edge line at row 82 follows, with dark shadow at rows 83-84. Below it is a weathered ashlar front face of about 62 rows (82-143). The towers and gatehouses each have their own crenellated platform top above a front face with arrow slits or doors, and the south wall repeats the same structure. The west and east walls read as flat tops seen from above, not receding side faces. This matches the 'cabinet: top 5 + edge + eave' pattern and not the 'rim only' or 'top-down slab' patterns.

styleAnswer.evidence: The ashlar faces and tower shafts carry about 5 grey steps. Blocks are shaded one by one, with mortar lines, cracks, a darker base course, a snow-lip highlight and a clear light/shadow side. The measured visible tones per tile are 11, against 12 and 10 for the references, so density is on par. Dark edge pixels are only 3% neutral, so the outlines lean toward the material tone, not a black sticker line. The weaker areas are the wall-walk snow and the road. These are broad, pale, lightly speckled surfaces with a few flat light-blue shadow bands, which is why near-flat coverage is 19% against 0% for the references. The speckle keeps them from reading as true flat fills. The stone, door, arch, banner and brazier details are rich enough that a careful artist would accept the piece next to the references. It is a little thinner than them in the open snow and road areas.

answer.evidence: The north wall has a snowy flagstone wall-walk top about 31-32 rows deep (rows 51-81, column x=303: parapet 51-63, snow 64-81). It ends in a front-edge line at row 82 with dark eave shadow at row 83. Below it is a weathered ashlar front face (rows 83-143, about 60 rows) with arrow slits and doors. The towers and gatehouses likewise show crenellated platform tops above their front faces. West and east walls are shown from above as walkway strips. The structure reads as three-quarter view, with every major part showing a top and a front face.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate matches the references on the primary facts: 11 visible tones per 16x16 tile against 12 and 10, and only 3% neutral dark edge pixels against 7% and 9%. Outlines lean towards the neighbouring material (grey-brown beside stone, blue-grey beside snow), so there is no black sticker line. The ashlar faces are shaded block by block in about 5 grey steps, with mortar lines, a darker base course, snow-capped crenellations and a shadow side on the towers. Details such as the wooden doors, banners, torches, shields and stairs add structure. Weaknesses: only 49 distinct colours overall, 19% near-flat coverage against 0% for the references, and the snow wall-walks and the road are fairly smooth, with only sparse speckle. The shading is slightly less rich than the Beodeul roofs, which carry per-tile highlights. These are minor, not shallow, and the wall-face tiles are about as dense as the stone reference.
